Bringing together a comprehensive city asset list, the grid reliability mapping, mapping of previous disaster impact areas, social vulnerability mapping through the then available Climate and Economic Justice Screening Tool and EPA EJScreen, and information gleaned from the tabletop exercises, the CIT took 4 months to develop a site scoring rubric to help identify the top city and community assets available for solar PV and storage development. To rank all assets, the developed rubric included considerations of energy usage, site topography and underlying characteristics, estimated potential array size, and resulting economic considerations. Using this rubric (Figure 5) and energy data from across City operations, the CIT narrowed down the best 10 sites for solar and storage. 12 Figure 5. Siting rubric (Appendix B) After the determination of the top sites were complete, an initial analysis of each site was completed by LHB Inc, an engineering firm contracted to do an initial assessment to ground-truth conclusions established through the siting rubric and further identify a smaller subset of sites for a second phase engineering design and deeper financial analysis. Diverse sites were identified for potential projects including a community center that could be repurposed as a resilience hub and the municipal gas utilities office/maintenance building. Out of the ten sites, the City’s Bayview Water Reservoir and Pump Station rose to the top as the most promising project for solar PV implementation and as a demonstration site to work through City processes for permitting, construction, and financial benefits structures. The City’s Bayview Water Reservoir and Pump Station, located at 6300 Highland Street was selected not only for the ability to reuse developed infrastructure but also because of the community in which it resides. The site is 0.25 miles from a redeveloped brownfield and is located directly adjacent to a low-moderate income (LMI) neighborhood (census tract 27137003300). This neighborhood was identified by Minnesota Power as a vulnerable area due to the high System Average Interruption Duration Index (SAIDI) and System Average Interruption Frequency Index (SAIFI) scores; which shows that this site is within neighborhoods with some of the most frequent and longer duration power losses in the Duluth community. A proposed project would use one of the City’s 10,000,000-gallon water reservoir and pump station sites to develop approximately 1-MW of solar with a portion of the solar used for pumping operations and the remainder available as a low-income community solar garden. The 6-acre site is host to an approximate 81,100 square foot concrete cap that is completely vacant, and recently replaced in 2014. Although using the site as a foundation for a neighborhood-based microgrid was dismissed as too expensive, solar installation provides positive secondary use of the site, takes advantage of capital improvement 13 investments on the cap, and increases blue sky financial stability for the city and participating low-income households. Duluth has historically been a hub for industry with limited availability of vacant land for large-scale solar within city limits. Incorporating solar onto existing assets reduces the City’s operating costs, carbon footprint, greenhouse gas emissions, and personnel time.
